performers: Philadelphia Orchestra, Leopold Stokowski (Stokowski’s own orchestration)
question: How does an orchestra redistribute the organ work’s attacks and sustained sound?
intro: This is the first disc side of Stokowski’s 1927 orchestral transcription of Bach’s organ work. Compare its opening with Norbert Schenk’s organ performance; the remainder of the 78-rpm recording is not joined to this stream.

cues.title: The conductor also orchestrates
cues.text: Stokowski’s transcription and its first recording date from 1927. The recording here predates Fantasia; it is not the film soundtrack.
cues.evidence: LA Phil identifies the transcription and first recording in 1927 and its selection for Fantasia in 1938; Commons dates this session 6 April 1927.

cues.title: Weight follows exposed gestures
cues.text: Across the opening, compare the spaces around the gestures with the fuller sound that follows. The orchestra and organ can sustain notes in different ways even when they trace the same musical outline.
cues.evidence: The 0:22 boundary precedes a rise from −18.7 dB at 0:15 to −8.9 at 0:25; the source identifies the orchestral medium.

cues.title: A renewed surge
cues.text: A quiet passage is followed by another strong surge. Follow the shape of the expansion, rather than treating the two recordings’ playback levels as equivalent dynamics.
cues.evidence: A 0:54 boundary follows low windows at 0:40–0:50 and leads to −5.3 dB at 1:00, one of this transfer’s highest windows.

cues.title: The later crest approaches
cues.text: The later passage grows towards the largest measured crest on this side. The comparison follows the opening only; it does not use the short side’s duration as a complete-work performance time.
cues.evidence: The highest relative-level window is 3:00 at −5.2 dB. The common passage ends at 180 seconds, before the later side continuation.

cues.title: A quieter continuation
cues.text: After the crest, the recording becomes markedly quieter. The side continues, but the automatic comparison no longer assigns this later passage to the organ performance.
cues.evidence: The 3:12 boundary lies in the fall from −7.5 dB at 3:05 to −25.1 at 3:10; the map ends before this region.

composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
